title: Zhang Fei's Roar at Changban Bridge: How Much Is Really in the Histories?
description:
The Records of the Three Kingdoms, in Zhang Fei's biography, already says Zhang Fei held the rear with twenty riders, held the river and cut the bridge, and challenged the enemy with his spear leveled, and none of them dared come near.
For viewers who want to tell the legend of "a roar that shook the bridge down" apart from what the histories actually say.

Liu Bei's biography also records that when Liu Bei fled, many of his followers and much of his baggage fell into Cao Cao's hands. It was the Romance of the Three Kingdoms that added the dust raised by branches tied to horses' tails, the three great shouts, Xiahou Jie falling from his horse, and the bridge torn down after the enemy withdrew, which only brought the pursuers back. This video sets the two texts side by side and asks: when did the bridge actually break, and who broke it?

The images are AI-generated cartoon illustrations, not reconstructions of the ancient battlefield, of anyone's appearance or of the bridge's construction. Main sources: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, volumes 32 and 36, and Pei Songzhi's annotations to volume 35; the Mao Zonggang commentary edition of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, chapters 41 and 42. Links to fixed versions of the original texts are listed below. Fact-checked on 2026-10-19.

eb001.text: Changban, Dangyang: Liu Bei flees; Zhang Fei holds the rear.

eb002.text: History says Zhang Fei held a bridge by the water with only a few riders.

eb003.text: The pursuers have caught up. What can these few riders win for Liu Bei?

eb004.text: History says the bridge was cut. Did a shout really break it?

eb005.text: In the record, how do they react to his challenge?

eb006.text: Why could Cao Cao's men chase him clear to Changban?

eb007.text: Before the chase reached Changban, Jingzhou changed: in Jian'an 13, 208 AD, Liu Biao died.

eb008.text: His heir, Liu Cong, gave in to Cao Cao.

eb009.text: Liu Bei was at Fancheng; only when Cao Cao reached Wan did he hear.

eb010.text: At Xiangyang, Zhuge Liang urged: strike Liu Cong now, take Jingzhou.

eb011.text: Liu Bei just said, "I cannot bear it," and didn't turn back to attack.

eb012.text: Leaving Fancheng, he first aimed for Jiangling.

eb013.text: But how many actually followed him?

eb014.text: At Xiangyang, Liu Cong's old men and Jingzhou folk joined him too.

eb015.text: A huge crowd followed, hauling masses of baggage.

eb016.text: Liu Bei's biography: at Dangyang, over 100,000 followed.

eb017.text: Thousands of carts, 10-odd li a day.

eb018.text: With so many carts and people, can they hurry?

eb019.text: Some urged: leave the people, rush to Jiangling; few can fight in armor.

eb020.text: Liu Bei said: they came with me. How could I abandon them?

eb021.text: He sent Guan Yu's fleet by water, to meet at Jiangling.

eb022.text: That slow on land: what would Cao Cao go for?

eb023.text: He'd keep Jiangling's war stores from Liu Bei.

eb024.text: Cao Cao left his wagons, racing light troops to Xiangyang.

eb025.text: Told Liu Bei was gone, he sent 5,000 crack cavalry.

eb026.text: How many reached the bridge, though, the histories don't say.

eb027.text: Liu Bei's biography: 300-plus li in a day and a night.

eb028.text: Where would fast horses catch the slow column?

eb029.text: At Dangyang's Changban, Liu Bei's men broke.

eb030.text: Leaving family, he fled with Zhuge Liang, Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun.

eb052.text: Zhao Yun's biography: he bore the infant heir and got Lady Gan to safety.

eb031.text: Cao seized many followers and carts.

eb032.text: They belong in the bridge legend too. So who could stay behind?

eb033.text: In that moment, Liu Bei gave Zhang Fei a job.

eb034.text: With how many riders can Zhang Fei stop them?

eb035.text: Zhang Fei's biography: twenty riders held the rear.

eb036.text: Then four characters, "held the river, cut the bridge": his post, the bridge's state.

eb037.text: It doesn't say who cut it, what the bridge was made of, or even when it broke.

eb038.text: After those four words, how did Zhang Fei halt the pursuit?

eb047.text: The biography never says what they feared. What trick will the novel fill it with?

eb054.text: The novel adds a grove by the bridge: Zhang Fei first eyes the east side.

eb055.text: His riders tie branches to horse tails and run laps in the woods.

eb056.text: Hooves and branches raise dust. What would distant pursuers take it for?

eb057.text: Wen Pin then reaches the bridge, first seeing dust behind the woods.

eb058.text: Suspecting an ambush, he reins in and goes no further.

eb059.text: Cao Ren and Zhang Liao arrive too, fearing a Zhuge Liang ruse.

eb060.text: They deploy west of the bridge and alert Cao Cao.

eb061.text: Word sent: will Cao Cao come himself?

eb062.text: In chapter 42, Cao Cao, too, reaches the bridge.

eb063.text: Zhang Fei sees a blue silk canopy far back: Cao Cao, he guesses.

eb039.text: Back to Zhang Fei's biography: "glaring, spear leveled": eyes fixed, spear across his chest.

eb040.text: It also records his exact words to the pursuers.

eb041.text: It reads: "I am Zhang Yide! Come fight me to the death!"

eb045.text: What those riders won is the biography's next line: "None of the enemy dared approach, so he escaped." Liu Bei got free.

eb043.text: History writes his name Yide with "benefit"; the novel, with "wing."

eb100.text: History gives one short challenge. How will the novel reword and amplify it?

eb064.text: The novel: "I am Zhang Yide of Yan! Who dares fight me to the death?" A voice like thunder.

eb065.text: Cao's troops' legs tremble, yet Cao Cao stays at the bridge.

eb066.text: Cao Cao quickly drops his canopy and warns: don't take him lightly.

eb067.text: Guan Yu once said Zhang Fei could behead generals amid great armies.

eb068.text: Zhang Fei roars again: dare they fight to the death?

eb069.text: Cao Cao is wavering; Zhang Fei sees his rear lines begin to move.

eb070.text: How else will Zhang Fei push them?

eb071.text: Zhang Fei shouts a third time: "Not fighting, not retreating: why?"

eb072.text: Mid-shout, a man by Cao Cao tumbles from his horse.

eb073.text: The novel gives him a name: Xiahou Jie.

eb074.text: Cao Cao turns, his troops follow: this too is the novel.

eb075.text: Zhang Liao, Xu Chu grab his reins; Cao Cao steadies some.

eb076.text: He sends them back to see what's happening on the bridge.

eb078.text: He has held the bridge. What will he do to it next?

eb079.text: No pursuit: he calls his riders back.

eb080.text: They drop the tail branches; he has the bridge torn down.

eb081.text: In the novel, that demolition brings new trouble.

eb082.text: Back with Liu Bei, Zhang Fei gets more than praise.

eb083.text: What worries him about the cut bridge?

eb084.text: You cut the bridge, he says; now Cao Cao knows there's no ambush.

eb085.text: Zhang Fei doubts it: he just roared them away. Why come back?

eb086.text: Sure enough, scouts Zhang Liao and Xu Chu report: bridge cut, Zhang Fei gone.

eb087.text: Cao Cao sees fear; three pontoons by nightfall.

eb088.text: Once those bridges are up, can Liu Bei still escape?

eb089.text: Li Dian fears another Zhuge Liang trick, but Cao Cao pushes on.

eb090.text: The novel corners Liu Bei at Hanjin: river ahead, enemies behind.

eb091.text: Who can stop Cao Cao first?

eb092.text: Then drums behind a hill: Guan Yu suddenly appears and blocks Cao's army.

eb093.text: Cao Cao fears a trap again and retreats; the chase the torn bridge drew finally stops.

eb046.text: Liu Bei's biography gives his next step: how did he cross?

eb049.text: He cut across to Hanjin and met Guan Yu's boats.

eb050.text: They crossed the Mian River and met Liu Qi's troops.

eb101.text: Remember the plan for Jiangling? Did they still go?

eb051.text: No. Instead of Jiangling, they went on together to Xiakou.

eb095.text: Back to our bridge: neither original text says a shout broke it.

eb096.text: If someone asks whether Changban Bridge is real, first ask: which line?

eb097.text: Put each line back in its book, and the bridge stands firm.

eb098.text: Which Three Kingdoms scene would you fact-check?

eb099.text: If you like history read against fiction, subscribe to the channel.
